item.text: {"facts":[{"source_id":"SRC-42d976481b68a6db","start_unit":3,"end_unit":5,"fact_summary":"López Obrador served as Mexico’s president from 1 December 2018 to 1 October 2024. His 2018 governing program emphasized republican austerity, poverty reduction, criminal-violence reduction, reduced internal military deployment subject to creating a National Guard, energy and food self-sufficiency, anti-corruption, and cooperative relations with the United States.","question_ids":["2B.10","3B.6","4B.10","5B.1","6B.1","8B.1","8B.2","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"context","period_fit":"The source establishes the ruler’s mandate and stated program but is updated only through 2018, not 2023.","ruler_attribution":"CIDOB attributes the program and presidency to Andrés Manuel López Obrador.","limitations":["The source does not establish 2023 implementation, expenditure, outcomes, or corrections."]},{"source_id":"SRC-42d976481b68a6db","start_unit":8,"end_unit":9,"fact_summary":"During his 2000–2005 tenure as head of government of Mexico City, López Obrador oversaw public-works expansion and social-protection programs, including a universal food pension for older adults; opponents alleged budgetary profligacy, while debt reportedly grew more slowly than under earlier governments. Crime-control results received mixed assessments.","question_ids":["3B.6","5B.6","6B.2","6B.3","6B.10","8B.6","8B.7"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"This concerns an earlier subnational tenure and is indirect context for 2023.","ruler_attribution":"CIDOB reports the policies and competing assessments of López Obrador’s Mexico City administration.","limitations":["No 2023 evidence; no quantified causal attribution or independent evaluation is supplied."]},{"source_id":"SRC-42d976481b68a6db","start_unit":9,"end_unit":10,"fact_summary":"In the 2004 video-corruption scandal, close López Obrador associates were filmed receiving large sums of money or negotiating political favors. López Obrador rejected the conduct but reacted late and mildly, characterized the scandal as a political conspiracy, and alleged involvement by domestic and U.S. actors; the source states that he himself was not directly implicated.","question_ids":["7B.1","7B.2","7B.5","7B.6","7B.9","7B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The events predate 2023 and provide historical integrity context only.","ruler_attribution":"CIDOB attributes the public response and allegations to López Obrador and reports the conduct of his associates.","limitations":["The source is a secondary biography and does not establish whether López Obrador knew of or benefited from the conduct."]},{"source_id":"SRC-42d976481b68a6db","start_unit":11,"end_unit":12,"fact_summary":"After the 2006 presidential election, López Obrador disputed the result, alleged irregularities, and initially pursued institutional remedies, but after the electoral tribunal ordered only a partial recount and later validated Felipe Calderón’s victory, he rejected the ruling, called Calderón illegitimate, organized resistance actions, and accepted a self-declared role as 'legitimate president' outside constitutional authority.","question_ids":["4B.1","4B.2","4B.4","4B.6","4B.8","6B.7","7B.1","7B.2","7B.7","8B.9"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"This is historical context from 2006, not evidence of conduct in 2023.","ruler_attribution":"CIDOB attributes the electoral challenge, rhetoric, and extra-institutional actions to López Obrador.","limitations":["The source also reports that international and domestic electoral observers found the process clean; it does not independently adjudicate every allegation."]},{"source_id":"SRC-42d976481b68a6db","start_unit":15,"end_unit":16,"fact_summary":"For the 2012 campaign, López Obrador stated goals including anti-corruption institutions, social programs, a 6% annual growth rate, 1.2 million jobs annually, food self-sufficiency, higher real minimum wages, universal education and health coverage, pensions, police professionalization, and gradual military withdrawal from internal security after replacement capacity was established.","question_ids":["3B.2","3B.6","4B.10","5B.1","5B.6","6B.1","6B.2","6B.9","8B.1","8B.2"],"polarity":"context","period_fit":"The source records a prior campaign program, not 2023 execution.","ruler_attribution":"CIDOB attributes these commitments to López Obrador and his 2012 coalition.","limitations":["No evidence here shows which commitments were enacted, funded, implemented, or achieved by 2023."]},{"source_id":"SRC-42d976481b68a6db","start_unit":16,"end_unit":16,"fact_summary":"After losing the 2012 election, López Obrador initially accepted the need to follow legal channels, submitted a 639-page electoral challenge, and sought annulment; after the electoral tribunal rejected the challenge, he continued to reject the ruling and invoked peaceful civil disobedience.","question_ids":["4B.1","4B.4","4B.8","6B.8","7B.2","7B.7","8B.9"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"This concerns 2012 and is historical context only.","ruler_attribution":"CIDOB attributes the legal challenge, subsequent rejection, and civil-disobedience position to López Obrador.","limitations":["The source does not establish whether the alleged electoral violations occurred."]},{"source_id":"SRC-42d976481b68a6db","start_unit":19,"end_unit":20,"fact_summary":"López Obrador’s 2018 program specified republican austerity, no new debt, gradual minimum-wage and pension increases, expanded domestic refining, review or reversal of parts of the energy reform, food and energy self-sufficiency, a National Guard with a stated goal of pacifying Mexico within three years, anti-corruption action, migrant protection, and respect for macroeconomic stability and Banco de México autonomy.","question_ids":["3B.6","4B.10","5B.1","5B.3","5B.6","6B.1","6B.2","6B.9","8B.1","8B.2","8B.6","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"context","period_fit":"The program was stated before the 2018–2024 presidency; it is relevant as a baseline but does not itself document 2023 results.","ruler_attribution":"CIDOB attributes the program and commitments to López Obrador and MORENA.","limitations":["No supplied unit provides 2023 budget execution, institutional implementation, outcome indicators, or adaptation evidence."]},{"source_id":"SRC-42d976481b68a6db","start_unit":20,"end_unit":20,"fact_summary":"López Obrador won the 2018 presidential election with 53.19% of the vote; the electoral tribunal validated the process. His coalition obtained majorities in both federal chambers, giving the incoming president substantial formal legislative authority.","question_ids":["4B.1","4B.2","4B.4","8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.9"],"polarity":"favorable","period_fit":"This establishes inherited formal authority at the start of the 2018–2024 period, not a 2023 event.","ruler_attribution":"CIDOB reports the election result, tribunal validation, and congressional seat totals.","limitations":["The source does not show how that authority was exercised in 2023."]}],"documents_with_no_material_fact":["SRC-5ab6ce418229e78d","SRC-00bdfe5578df0f95","SRC-de19c6a8d761bcfe"],"batch_limitations":["The World Bank document units supplied concern countries other than Mexico and contain no material fact about López Obrador in 2023.","The supplied nuclear-convention and Sixth Government Report documents contain only challenge-validation text, without substantive extracted content.","The substantive CIDOB source is a historical biography updated through 2018; it provides program and historical context but no direct 2023 evidence."]}
